projects.functionalBrief: Proposed Design for a premium office interior supporting focused individual work, team collaboration, client meetings and informal staff exchange. The layout gives employees a legible shared address while containing noise around meeting and work rooms; reception, pantry and building services support daily operations without crossing the principal circulation route.
projects.floorOrSiteOrganization: Within a single assumed office floor plate, place reception at the lift lobby and extend a straight internal street to a central forum. Work neighbourhoods occupy daylit perimeter zones; meeting and focus rooms form acoustically buffered clusters along the spine, with pantry and print points close to teams but outside quiet rooms. Maintain a continuous accessible route to two separated existing protected stairs and the building core; final egress widths, occupant load and fire separation require coordination with the base building and local code.
projects.areaOrScale: Approx. 1,100–1,400 m² interior fit-out on one level for about 90–120 workpoints, meeting capacity for 35–45 people and a central forum for around 30; all areas, capacities and dimensions are proposal-stage assumptions subject to measured survey and applicable code.
projects.structuralSystem: Interior fit-out assumes an existing reinforced-concrete or composite office frame on an approximately 8–9 m planning grid, with perimeter columns and a central core retained. No new long-span structural canopy is proposed: the ribbed ceiling is a lightweight suspended acoustic-metal assembly on secondary hangers, coordinated around existing beams, sprinklers and services.
projects.constructionLogic: Survey and protect the landlord structure and services first; install demountable metal-stud and glazed partitions, then suspended acoustic ceiling zones, floor finish and joinery. Support the smoked-oak fronts and reeded acoustic glazing on independent subframes, provide accessible service hatches, and keep heavy granite limited to the circulation spine after checking floor loading. Coordinate ceiling ribs, clerestory interfaces, lighting, detectors and sprinklers before closing ceilings; use replaceable planting troughs with drained, waterproofed liners.
projects.environmentalResponse: Use existing shaded perimeter glazing and clerestory bands for diffuse daylight, with vertical fins or internal blinds at low-angle sun exposures and glare-controlled task lighting. Keep workstations near daylight and meeting rooms in deeper zones; specify acoustic ceiling absorption and efficient zoned lighting and cooling. Interior planting is limited to maintainable pockets with contained irrigation and drainage; retain existing base-building ventilation and verify fresh-air rates and controls during fit-out coordination.

projects.functionalBrief: Proposed Design for an interior-design scope within a private residence, not a new architectural commission: the work develops the domestic room sequence, finishes, built-in storage, lighting and thresholds around the preserved planted court. The interior should support family gathering, cooking, dining, quiet retreat and household service, with durable finishes and discreet storage for everyday operations.
projects.floorOrSiteOrganization: Treat the existing/planned single-storey pavilion arrangement as the fixed interior envelope, with public living and dining opening to the rain-tree court and private bedrooms reached from a quieter side passage. Keep kitchen, pantry, laundry and service access near one another and provide a discreet route to the external service edge; use the court as the orientation point, not as a circulation shortcut through private rooms. Maintain clear door swings and accessible thresholds between basalt interior floors and terracotta court paving; coordinate exits and fire provisions with the host building design.
projects.areaOrScale: Approx. 260–320 m² of interior-design scope across one level, comprising roughly 8–10 principal rooms/functions for a household of 4–6 plus visitors; dimensions and room areas are proposal-stage allowances dependent on measured base-building drawings.
projects.structuralSystem: Interior design assumes a low-rise host building with conventional reinforced-concrete or steel roof supports and masonry or framed walls; the folded roof, primary structure and court dimensions remain by the base-building architect/engineer. Teak screens, joinery and any non-load-bearing partitions are secondary fit-out elements, not structural supports for the roof.
projects.constructionLogic: Verify slab levels, damp-proofing, court falls and concealed services before setting out the continuous basalt finish. Install lime-plaster substrate and wet-area waterproofing before stone and teak joinery; use movement joints at long stone runs and flexible, drained thresholds at glazed openings. Fix vertical teak screens to corrosion-resistant brackets with replaceable slats and maintainable clearances; coordinate roof-drain outlets and overflow paths with the architect so concealed channels can be inspected and never discharge into the interior.
projects.environmentalResponse: Use the planted court and shaded openings for borrowed daylight and cross-ventilation where privacy, security and outdoor conditions permit; retain operable screened openings and ceiling fans as low-energy support. Deep eaves and teak screens limit direct sun and monsoon splash, while lime-based finishes and locally appropriate stone provide robust, repairable surfaces. Detail the court for positive drainage, rain-tree root space and controlled irrigation; mechanical cooling and ventilation in enclosed bedrooms and kitchen remain coordinated with the building services design.

projects.functionalBrief: Proposed Design for an interior-design package focused on the principal living space of a private residence, preserving the existing shell while coordinating finishes, lighting, stair and mezzanine detailing, and furniture. It supports family relaxation, hosting, reading and circulation between the living level, upper landing and garden, with safe stair use and unobstructed accessible movement at the main floor.
programme: Mezzanine reading or informal work area
projects.floorOrSiteOrganization: Keep the principal seating group central to the double-height room and orient it toward garden glazing; locate the stair along a solid side wall so its landing does not bisect the living route. The mezzanine overlooks the room but remains a secondary quiet zone with a guarded edge, while the kitchen/dining approach stays direct and furniture-free at the garden threshold. Preserve clear paths from entry to garden and stair, coordinate the upper-level escape route with the host building plan, and verify required guard, stair and glazing safety dimensions under applicable code.
projects.areaOrScale: Approx. 90–125 m² of interior-design scope over two connected levels, including a 35–50 m² double-height living room and a 15–25 m² mezzanine, for a household gathering of about 6–10 people; all dimensions are approximate proposal-stage assumptions.
projects.structuralSystem: Assume an existing reinforced-concrete or steel-framed residential shell with the mezzanine supported by engineered steel or timber secondary beams spanning between verified structural walls/columns. The floating-stair appearance is achieved with a concealed steel spine or paired stringers and individually fixed timber treads, with the engineer verifying deflection, vibration, anchorage and guard loads; it is not an unsupported cantilevered stair.
projects.constructionLogic: Survey the shell and confirm slab edges, stair opening, glazing and service routes before fabrication. Install mezzanine secondary framing and stair steel after structural sign-off, then fit timber treads, guard/handrail and oak flooring with movement gaps; anchor ceiling slats to a level service batten system rather than to finish plaster. Sequence glazing seals, floor transitions, joinery and lighting so concealed wiring remains accessible; provide a continuous handrail, slip-resistant treads, safe riser/going geometry and compliant guard height subject to local review.
projects.environmentalResponse: Use the garden-facing glazing for daylight and views, with exterior shade or operable blinds calibrated to orientation to control glare and solar gain; avoid placing screens or tall furniture across the daylight path. The double-height volume can support high-level heat relief only if safe, operable openings and insect control are available; otherwise retain the building's mechanical ventilation and cooling strategy. Specify dimmable layered lighting, efficient luminaires and low-emission timber finishes, and coordinate any planting irrigation and drainage outside the interior scope.

projects.functionalBrief: Proposed Design for a contemporary restaurant interior serving seated dining with both intimate tables and a shared communal option, while keeping kitchen service efficient and visible only in controlled glimpses. Staff need a direct route between prep, cooking, pass and dining, robust cleanable finishes, acoustic comfort and a discreet waste/service path; guests need a legible accessible entry, clear seating choices and convenient washrooms.
projects.floorOrSiteOrganization: Organize the narrow rectangular tenancy from street entry toward the rear planted court, with dining on the public side and the service spine separating seating from the open kitchen. Place the host point near the entry, keep the communal table visible but outside the principal aisle, and route staff from kitchen pass to tables without crossing the accessible guest route. Locate washrooms and storage near the back-of-house edge; maintain a separate kitchen delivery/waste route where the shell allows, and coordinate occupant load, accessible seating, kitchen exhaust, fire separation and two-way egress requirements with the building and code consultant.
projects.areaOrScale: Approx. 180–240 m² interior fit-out on one level for about 55–75 dining seats, including roughly 75–95 m² dining, 50–65 m² kitchen/back-of-house and guest support; exact seat count and floor area are approximate proposal-stage targets pending code, kitchen consultant and measured survey.
projects.structuralSystem: Assume an existing commercial shell with reinforced-concrete columns/walls or a regular steel frame at approximately 6–8 m bays; retain the structure and coordinate the long room around fixed supports. The terracotta baffles are lightweight suspended acoustic elements carried by secondary ceiling channels, while the skylight is an existing or separately engineered roof opening, not a new unsupported cut through primary structure.
projects.constructionLogic: Confirm slab capacity, roof waterproofing, grease/exhaust routes and existing fire services before detailed setting out. Form kitchen partitions and washable wet-area substrates first, then install Kota stone with falls and movement joints, lime plaster, service-spine joinery and ceiling suspension. Provide independent support and seismic restraint for terracotta baffles, maintain access to sprinklers and ducts, use tested non-combustible or fire-rated assemblies where required, and detail the linear skylight with curb, flashing, condensation control and accessible drainage. Grease trap, hood and exhaust discharge must be coordinated with building management and local approvals.
projects.environmentalResponse: Use recessed lane openings with external fins for diffuse daylight and limited natural ventilation when outdoor air quality, noise and security permit; the central skylight requires glare control and solar-diffusing glazing. Terracotta baffles with absorptive backing reduce reverberation, while efficient zoned lighting supplements daylight without hot spots on tables. The rear court can provide planted outlook and manage modest roof/runoff flows only with a designed overflow and maintainable drain; kitchen extraction and make-up air remain mechanically controlled and separate from guest comfort ventilation.

projects.functionalBrief: Proposed Design for a compact cultural gallery interior accommodating rotating exhibitions, small educational groups and visitor orientation, with flexible display infrastructure and controlled daylight for sensitive works. Staff require secure receiving and storage, simple exhibit changeover and clear supervision; visitors need an intuitive, step-free circuit, accessible facilities and a calm sequence from entry to galleries and courtyard.
projects.floorOrSiteOrganization: Arrange the visitor circuit around the narrow lightwell, with the entry bay acting as orientation and a continuous loop returning visitors toward exit without dead ends. Place galleries along the perimeter where screened openings provide controlled ambient light; locate storage, preparation, staff and receiving functions on the less public edge near service access. Keep the garden court outside the enclosed circulation route, maintain step-free turning and clearances, and provide a direct, independently legible egress path from each occupied gallery to compliant exits. Final occupancy, travel distances, fire compartmentation and collection-security provisions require local review.
projects.areaOrScale: Approx. 380–520 m² of gallery interior across one level surrounding an approximately 30–50 m² open-to-sky court, with 3–4 exhibition/learning rooms and a typical simultaneous visitor capacity of about 60–90; all room sizes and capacity are proposal-stage estimates subject to code and exhibit planning.
projects.structuralSystem: Assume a low-rise reinforced-concrete frame or load-bearing masonry host building with perimeter columns/walls and a regular 5–7 m planning grid. The entrance vault is a shallow engineered masonry or concrete finish form supported by the primary structure, not a free-standing shell; gallery partitions are non-load-bearing and can be repositioned without altering the structure. Perforated sandstone screens require engineered brackets and verified support loads at the façade.
projects.constructionLogic: Survey the existing structure and confirm court waterproofing, roof drainage, daylight openings and service routes before fixing gallery datums. Build the wet-area and lightwell upstands with continuous waterproofing, protected membrane and accessible drains/overflow; install stone floors with flush transitions and movement joints. Apply breathable mineral plaster to prepared substrates, mount replaceable exhibit walls on stable tracks or floor/ceiling channels, and support sandstone screens on corrosion-resistant fixings with movement allowance. Coordinate track lighting, emergency lighting, detection, sprinklers and flexible power/data before ceilings close; specify tested fire-rated finishes and secure, lockable collection storage.
projects.environmentalResponse: Orient and screen perimeter apertures to deliver reflected rather than direct sun; use the perforated sandstone as an external solar filter and blackout-capable internal shades where conservation needs demand. The lightwell brings soft top light and a planted outlook but should have controllable shading and high-level rain drainage; avoid using it as the only route for required ventilation. Use efficient dimmable track lighting with exhibit-specific controls, limit UV and heat gain, and provide stable mechanical temperature/humidity where collection requirements warrant it. Select a drought-adapted court tree and gravel planting with contained irrigation, overflow drainage and safe maintenance access.

projects.functionalBrief: Proposed Design for a hospitality lounge interior that provides a comfortable transition from wet-weather arrival to relaxed seating and a sheltered coastal verandah. Guests need varied conversational seating, clear views and accessible routes; staff need a discreet service point, storage and a durable cleaning strategy, with finishes able to withstand humidity, wind-driven rain and frequent use.
projects.floorOrSiteOrganization: Maintain the entry-to-verandah sequence from a compact sheltered vestibule through the salon to broad coastal openings. Arrange curved low seating as small islands while preserving a direct step-free route between arrival, service counter, washroom and verandah; position staff storage and service access behind or beside the counter rather than through guest seating. Keep the sea-view axis open and provide an alternate protected route back to the host building exit; verify guards, egress, wind exposure and accessible thresholds with the base-building design.
projects.areaOrScale: Approx. 140–190 m² interior fit-out on one level, with a 75–105 m² enclosed lounge, 35–55 m² covered verandah and capacity for roughly 35–50 seated guests; areas and capacity are proposal-stage estimates, with verandah area counted separately from enclosed floor area.
projects.structuralSystem: Assume an existing low-rise hospitality shell with reinforced-concrete or steel primary frame and a coastal roof structure. The shallow timber ceiling is a non-structural interior lining on a ventilated secondary batten system; the deep verandah eave and any roof extension must be supported by the building's engineered columns, rafters or cantilever beams, not by decorative ceiling boards. Laterite wall finishes are cladding or finish layers unless a structural engineer confirms otherwise.
projects.constructionLogic: Confirm wind-driven rain exposure, salt-air corrosion class, slab levels and roof drainage before selecting fixings and finishes. Install waterproofed vestibule and verandah thresholds with positive outward falls, linear drains and accessible overflow paths; use slip-resistant flamed stone and flexible joints at exterior transitions. Mechanically fix timber boards to ventilated battens with concealed corrosion-resistant fasteners, seal end grain and permit inspection; protect cane panels from direct wetting and provide replaceable upholstery. Test operable screens and door hardware, and detail roof gutters, downpipes and rain-court discharge for intense monsoon events.
projects.environmentalResponse: Use broad operable openings on opposing sides for cross-ventilation when wind-driven rain and humidity conditions allow, with woven screens and deep eaves to moderate glare and rain entry. Keep the horizon-facing view clear while controlling low sun through adjustable external screens; ceiling fans support comfort during mixed-mode operation. Specify moisture-tolerant, repairable finishes, ventilated timber backing and salt-resistant metal hardware; provide mechanical dehumidification or cooling when outdoor conditions require it. Capture roof runoff only through sized gutters and filtered storage/landscape overflow, using salt-tolerant planting in drained rain courts and planters.

projects.functionalBrief: Proposed Design for a contemporary retail interior that supports browsing, product presentation, fitting and checkout within a clear and welcoming customer journey. Staff need sightlines across low displays, secure stock and an efficient replenishment route; visitors need accessible circulation, fitting privacy, legible returns to the entrance and durable finishes suited to a humid coastal setting.
projects.floorOrSiteOrganization: Set the checkout and welcome point near the entrance with views down the long retail floor. A browsing loop circles the central basalt plinth and low islands; a side passage leads to fitting rooms and stockroom, keeping customer circulation distinct from staff replenishment wherever possible. Provide an accessible clear route to the fitting suite and exit, preserve turning space at display ends, and avoid placing merchandise in the required egress path. Coordinate retail occupant load, emergency lighting, exits, security and accessible fitting-room requirements with the host building and local code.
projects.areaOrScale: Approx. 160–220 m² interior fit-out on one level, including about 105–145 m² sales floor, 25–35 m² stock/support and 3–5 fitting rooms, with typical simultaneous customer capacity of roughly 25–40; figures are approximate proposal-stage planning assumptions subject to survey and code review.
projects.structuralSystem: Assume an existing one-storey or podium retail shell with reinforced-concrete columns/walls on an approximately 6–8 m grid and a suspended ceiling zone. Retain primary structure; the ash lattice ceiling is a lightweight suspended finish fixed to secondary channels, while display islands, brass-mesh partitions and basalt plinth are non-structural interior components. Verify floor loading and anchorage for the dense stone plinth and any freestanding display elements.
projects.constructionLogic: Complete measured survey, electrical/data plan and stockroom/fitting-room set-out before ordering modular displays. Prepare the floor substrate for terrazzo or compatible hard-wearing finish with control joints, then install fixed joinery and a mechanically supported basalt plinth with concealed safe edges. Suspend the ash lattice from an independently levelled subframe, coordinate its glazed daylight slot with existing roof waterproofing and fire services, and make panels removable for access. Fix brass mesh within framed panels with smooth protected edges; waterproof the rain-garden interface, provide a drained threshold and keep rill maintenance and overflow outside the public circulation line.
projects.environmentalResponse: Use side openings screened by vertical fins and the narrow ceiling daylight slot for soft ambient light, supplemented by high-CRI efficient track lighting with controls by zone. Limit direct sun and product fading with external shade and UV-conscious glazing; avoid glare on the basalt feature surface and fitting-room mirrors. Operable openings may provide shoulder-season fresh air where outdoor humidity, security and acoustic conditions permit, while mechanical cooling and dehumidification serve humid periods. The rain garden receives only controlled roof runoff through maintainable drains and overflow, with moisture-tolerant planting and a safe barrier or edge detail at the shallow rill.
